Week 7: Industrial Sensors & Logic

EE0849 Introduction to Robotics

Basri Erdogan

Part 1: Digital I/O Fundamentals

The Robot’s Nervous System

Robots interact with the world through digital I/O — simple ON/OFF signals at 24V DC. Analog I/O also exists (force sensors, variable-speed drives) but digital covers most factory use cases.

Digital Inputs: NPN vs PNP

What robots sense: part presence, position confirmation, safety status, machine states

When wiring sensors, match the type: PNP is standard in Europe/Asia (our lab), NPN in North America. Wrong type → input never triggers.

NPN and PNP refer to the output transistor type inside the sensor. Both are 3-wire sensors (brown = +24V, blue = 0V, black = signal).

PNP (sourcing): When the sensor detects something, it connects the signal wire to +24V internally. The controller input sees +24V = ON. The current flows FROM the sensor TO the controller input, then to ground through the input card. The sensor is the “source” of current.

NPN (sinking): When the sensor detects something, it connects the signal wire to 0V (ground) internally. The controller input is pulled to ground = ON. The current flows FROM the +24V supply through the input card TO the sensor, then to ground. The sensor is the “sink” — it provides the path to ground.

Why it matters: Our FANUC controller has PNP-compatible inputs (it expects to see +24V when active). If you accidentally buy an NPN sensor, the input will never read ON — or worse, it might float and give false readings. Always check the sensor datasheet for “PNP” or “sourcing” output.

Quick way to remember: PNP = Positive output when active. NPN = Negative (ground) output when active.

Digital Outputs

What robots control: grippers, conveyors, indicator lights, other machines

Type Use case Example
Transistor Fast DC switching Gripper valve, 24V light
Relay Isolation, AC/DC 220V conveyor, separate power supply
Triac AC loads, no wear AC cooling fan, heater element

Our FANUC has transistor outputs (24V DC) — sufficient for grippers and lights. For heavier loads, wire the DO to an external relay or contactor.

FANUC I/O Architecture

Type Inputs Outputs Location
Digital (DI/DO) DI[1]–DI[8] DO[1]–DO[8] Controller cabinet
Robot (RI/RO) RI[1]–RI[8] RO[1]–RO[8] On the robot arm
User (UI/UO) UI[1]–UI[18] UO[1]–UO[10] Safety / status
Group (GI/GO) GI[1]–GI[N] GO[1]–GO[N] Multi-bit (integers)

Accessing I/O in TP Programs:

  • Read input: IF DI[1]=ON, ...
  • Set output: DO[1]=ON
  • Wait for input: WAIT DI[2]=ON

Students may ask about the difference between DI, RI, and UI:

DI/DO (Digital I/O): Physical wires connected to the controller’s I/O board in the cabinet. These are the ones we use for sensors and actuators in the workcell — a proximity sensor on DI[1], a gripper solenoid on DO[1], etc.

RI/RO (Robot I/O): Signals mapped to connectors on the robot arm itself (not the controller cabinet). Used for end-effector devices wired through the robot arm, like a gripper solenoid valve mounted on the wrist. The wiring runs through the arm’s internal cable bundle.

UI/UO (User Operator Panel I/O): Signals tied to operator panel functions — start, stop, hold, fault reset. In a factory, these are wired to a PLC or custom operator panel so an external system can start/stop the robot remotely. For example, UI[18] = “External Start” from a PLC. Our education cell doesn’t have a physical operator panel, so these signals are virtual — you can see them under MENU → I/O → UOP but they’re not wired to anything.

GI/GO (Group I/O): Multi-bit signals that carry integer values (e.g., 8-bit group = values 0–255). Used for communicating part numbers, recipe IDs, or station codes with a PLC.

For our lab, we only use DI/DO.

Part 2: Industrial Sensors

Proximity Sensors

Barrel-shaped M12/M30, mounts flush in a bracket — you’ll see dozens on any factory line.

Inductive — detects metal only

  • “Is the steel bolt in the fixture?”
  • Range: 1–30 mm, response: <1 ms
  • Cheap, fast, very reliable

Capacitive — detects any material (metal, plastic, liquid, wood)

  • Glue level in a reservoir, plastic cap presence
  • Range: 1–25 mm
  • Sensitive to environment (humidity, dust)

Photoelectric Sensors

All use light (infrared/visible) to detect objects at a distance.

Type Use case Range
Through-Beam Box counting, gate up to 30 m
Retro-Reflective Pallet detection 3–10 m
Diffuse PCB on tray? 10–500 mm

Mechanical & Pressure Sensors

  • Limit Switch: Physical contact — object pushes lever, toggles contacts (NO↔︎NC). Confirms clamp closed, end-of-travel. Nearly indestructible.
  • Pressure Switch: Monitors pneumatic line pressure — if pressure drops, DI goes OFF → fault detected.
  • Vacuum Switch: Measures suction level at the gripper. If vacuum is below threshold → part not sealed → abort pick.

How the vacuum switch works with a suction gripper:

A vacuum gripper picks parts by suction — a vacuum pump pulls air through the suction cup, creating negative pressure that holds the part against the cup. When the cup seals properly against the part, the vacuum level rises (e.g., to -60 kPa). When there’s no part or the seal is bad (wrong shape, porous surface), the vacuum level stays low (e.g., -10 kPa) because air keeps leaking in.

The vacuum switch (like the SMC ZSE30 in the image) is a small digital pressure sensor connected to the suction line. You set a threshold (e.g., -40 kPa). When vacuum reaches that threshold, the switch outputs ON (24V on its signal wire → DI goes ON). The TP program checks this:

DO[1:Vacuum]=ON ;          ! Turn on vacuum pump
WAIT 0.50(sec) ;            ! Give time to build vacuum
IF DI[2:Vac_OK]=OFF, JMP LBL[99] ;  ! No seal → abort
L P[2:Lift] 200mm/sec FINE ;         ! Seal OK → lift part

Without this check, the robot might lift with a bad seal and drop a glass panel mid-air. The vacuum switch is essentially a “grip confirm” sensor for suction grippers, just like a force sensor confirms grip for finger grippers.

Limit switch details: Has three terminals: C (common), NO (normally open), NC (normally closed). When the lever is not pressed, C-NC is connected. When pressed, C-NO is connected. Wire to whichever logic you need. For safety applications (e.g., confirming a guard door is closed), use the NC contact — if the wire breaks, the circuit opens, which is the safe state.

Other Sensor Types

Beyond the four main types, you will encounter these in robotics:

  • Encoders — Inside every servo motor; measure joint position and velocity. The robot already uses these — they’re how the controller knows the current joint angles
  • Force/Torque (F/T) — Mounted at the wrist; measures 6-axis contact forces. Used for assembly, polishing, and collision detection
  • Vision / Camera — 2D or 3D imaging for part localization, inspection, and guidance. We will use iRVision in a later lab
  • Ultrasonic — Distance measurement using sound waves. Used for bin fill level, object distance (1 cm – several meters)
  • Laser distance / ToF — Precise ranging and profiling (e.g., part height inspection, surface scanning)
  • Pressure / Flow — Confirms pneumatic gripper pressure, coolant flow, vacuum level

Sensor Selection Guide

Sensor Type Detects Range Speed Cost
Inductive Metal only Short Fast Low
Capacitive Any material Short Medium Medium
Photoelectric Any (line of sight) Long Fast Medium
Limit Switch Physical contact Contact Slow Low

Selection Criteria:

  1. What material? (Metal → Inductive)
  2. What range? (Long → Photoelectric)
  3. Environment? (Dirty → Inductive/Limit)
  4. Speed required? (Fast → Inductive/Photo)

Quick Check: Sensor Selection

Scenario: Your robot cell needs to detect:

  1. Steel bolts arriving on a conveyor (range ~5mm)
  2. A cardboard box at a loading station (range ~2m)
  3. Whether the gripper jaws are fully closed

Answers:

  1. Inductive proximity — metal, short range, fast, cheap
  2. Photoelectric (retro-reflective) — any material, long range
  3. Limit switch — mechanical contact, confirms physical position

Real Sensors for the FANUC ER-4iA

Any 3-wire PNP sensor with 24V DC output wires directly to DI[1]–DI[8].

Need Sensor Type Example Models
Metal part in fixture Inductive (M8/M12 barrel) Omron E2E, Sick IME, IFM IF5
Any-material detection Diffuse photoelectric Omron E3Z, Sick W4, Banner QS18
Gripper closed confirm Micro limit switch Omron D4MC, Honeywell V15
Suction grip confirm Vacuum switch SMC ZSE30, Festo VPEV
Cell entry detection Safety light curtain Sick C4000, Omron F3SG

For a basic pick-and-place cell you typically need just 2–3 sensors: one for part presence (inductive), one for grip confirm (pressure/vacuum switch), and optionally one at the place station (diffuse photoelectric).

Part 3: Safety Systems

Why Safety is Critical

Safety is not optional — it’s regulated by law (ISO 10218, ANSI/RIA 15.06, EN ISO 13849). Every robot cell must address these four hazard categories through layered protection.

Industrial robots are powerful machines — a typical 6-axis arm can move at over 2 m/s and exert hundreds of newtons of force. Unlike a power tool that a human holds and controls directly, a robot moves autonomously through programmed paths, which means a person nearby may not be able to predict or dodge its motion.

The four hazard categories on this slide — impact/crushing, pinch points, ejected parts, and electrical/environmental — cover the vast majority of recorded incidents. Impact and crushing injuries are the most common: the robot swings into a worker who entered the cell during automatic mode. Pinch points are subtler — fingers or clothing caught between the robot and a fixture, or between two moving links. Ejected parts happen when a gripper loses a workpiece at speed. Electrical and environmental hazards include arc flash from welding robots, chemical exposure from paint or adhesive dispensing, and high-temperature burns.

Key point to emphasize: safety is not just good practice, it is a legal requirement. ISO 10218-1 covers the robot itself, ISO 10218-2 covers the robot cell and integration, and ISO/TS 15066 adds requirements specific to collaborative robots. In Turkey, the relevant regulation is the İş Ekipmanlarının Kullanımında Sağlık ve Güvenlik Şartları Yönetmeliği. Non-compliance can result in facility shutdowns, fines, and criminal liability if someone is injured.

The philosophy is “layered protection” (defense in depth): no single device is trusted alone. We combine physical barriers, electronic sensing, control-reliable circuits, and operational procedures so that if any one layer fails, the others still protect the worker.

Safety Circuit Architecture

The diagram says it all: every device is NC and wired in series. Any break → robot stops. No software can override this chain.

The key idea on this slide is the series NC (normally closed) chain. Every safety device sits as a normally closed contact in one continuous loop. In the normal “safe to run” state, all contacts are closed and current flows through the entire chain to the safety relay, which in turn enables motor power. The moment any single device opens its contact — someone presses E-Stop, a beam is broken, someone steps on the mat — the loop breaks and the safety relay de-energizes the motor power supply. This is fail-safe by design: a broken wire, a lost signal, or a power failure all look the same as a triggered device — the circuit opens and the robot stops.

Our lab setup: Our FANUC LR Mate 200iD does not have all the elements shown in this diagram. We don’t have a light curtain, a safety mat, or a physical fence enclosure. What we do have is: the E-Stop buttons (on the teach pendant and on the controller panel), the deadman switch (3-position enable on the pendant), the mode switch (T1/T2/AUTO), and the controller’s built-in safety relay board. Our safety chain is shorter — E-Stop contacts and deadman in series through the safety relay to motor power — but the principle is identical. The missing perimeter devices would simply add more NC contacts in the same series loop. In our lab, the compensation for not having perimeter guarding is operational: we always work in T1 mode (250 mm/s limit), always hold the deadman, and keep bystanders at a safe distance. This is acceptable for an educational cell with supervised access, but would not be sufficient for a production environment.

How the safety mat works: A safety mat is a pressure-sensitive pad placed on the floor around the robot cell. It consists of two conductive plates separated by a compressible insulating spacer. When no one is standing on it, the plates are apart and the mat’s relay holds the safety circuit closed (safe to run). When someone steps onto the mat, their weight compresses the plates together, the mat’s relay detects this change and opens the NC contact in the safety chain, stopping the robot. Crucially, if a person faints and collapses onto the mat, their body weight still compresses the plates — the robot stays stopped. The mat doesn’t care whether you’re standing, kneeling, or lying down; it responds purely to pressure. The robot cannot restart until the weight is removed and the circuit is explicitly reset. The limitation is coverage area: the mat only protects the zone it physically covers, so mat placement and sizing must ensure that a person cannot reach the robot’s workspace without stepping on the mat first.

Safety Devices

Device How It Works Trigger
E-Stop Red mushroom button, hardwired Pressed → cuts power
Deadman 3-position enable switch Release or squeeze = stop
Light Curtain IR beam array across opening Body breaks beam → stop
Safety Mat Pressure-sensitive floor Person steps on → stop

FANUC Operating Modes

Mode Speed Deadman Use
T1 (Teach) ≤ 250 mm/s Must hold Teaching positions, testing
T2 (Test) Full speed Must hold Full-speed verification
AUTO (Run) Full speed Not used Production, cycle start via UI[6]
  • T1 → T2 → AUTO progression: always test at slow speed first
  • Mode selected by key switch on controller
  • Deadman switch: release OR squeeze fully = immediate stop

Part 4: Motion & Position Fundamentals

Motion Types

Type Syntax Path Shape Speed Units When to Use
Joint (J) J P[1] 100% FINE Curved (joint space) % of max (1–100) Large free moves, fastest
Linear (L) L P[2] 500mm/sec FINE Straight line mm/sec, cm/min Near workpieces, precise
Circular (C) C P[3] P[4] 200mm/sec FINE Arc through via point mm/sec, cm/min Curved paths (welding, sealing)
Arc (A) A P[5] 200mm/sec FINE Chained circular arcs mm/sec, cm/min Continuous curves (3+ arc segments)
  • J moves all joints simultaneously — path is unpredictable in Cartesian space
  • L and C control the TCP path — the controller interpolates in Cartesian space
  • A requires 3+ consecutive arc instructions to define the full curve

Speed Control

Motion Unit Range Example
Joint (J) % 1–100 J P[1] 50% FINE
Linear (L, C, A) mm/sec 1–2000 L P[2] 800mm/sec CNT50
Linear (L, C, A) cm/min 1–12000 L P[2] 4800cm/min CNT50
Rotation deg/sec 1–272 L P[3] 90deg/sec FINE
Any sec 0.1–3200 L P[4] 2.0sec FINE

Override: limits all motion to a percentage of programmed speed:

OVERRIDE=50% ;     ! All moves run at half speed
OVERRIDE=R[10]% ;  ! Speed from register

Termination Types: FINE vs CNT

L P[1] 100mm/sec FINE    ; Stop exactly at point
L P[2] 500mm/sec CNT50   ; Blend through point

Rule of thumb: FINE at pick/place, CNT for transit.

  • CNT0 = closest to point without stopping
  • CNT100 = maximum smoothing (fastest, least accurate)
  • Blending is faster but the robot won’t hit the exact waypoint

Position Data

Cartesian representation:

UF:2  UT:1
X:  1500.374  W:  10.000
Y: -342.992  P:  20.000
Z:  956.895  R:  40.000
CONF: N, U, T, 0, 0, 0
  • X, Y, Z — TCP position (mm)
  • W, P, R — orientation (degrees)
  • CONF — robot configuration

Joint representation:

J1:   45.000   J4:    0.000
J2:  -30.000   J5:  -90.000
J3:   60.000   J6:  180.000
  • Each value is one joint angle (degrees)
  • No ambiguity — one set of joint values = one pose
  • Used internally for J motion

Robot Configuration

The same Cartesian pose (X,Y,Z,W,P,R) can be reached with multiple joint solutions — the configuration string resolves this ambiguity.

Flag Options Meaning
Wrist FLIP / NOFLIP Wrist orientation (J5 sign)
Arm UP / DOWN Elbow above or below shoulder line
Reach FRONT / BACK Robot reaching forward or backward
Turn –1, 0, 1 Which 360° sector each axis is in 
CONF: N, U, T, 0, 0, 0
       │  │  │  │  │  └─ J6 turn number
       │  │  │  │  └──── J5 turn number
       │  │  │  └─────── J4 turn number
       │  │  └────────── FRONT (T) or BACK (B)
       │  └───────────── UP (U) or DOWN (D)
       └──────────────── NOFLIP (N) or FLIP (F)

This is the IK solution selector — same target, different arm pose.

P[i] vs PR[i]

P[i] — Position Variable PR[i] — Position Register
Scope Local to one program Global (shared across all programs)
Typical use Taught waypoints Computed positions, offsets
How set Teach pendant (jog & record) TP code or direct entry
Count Up to ~5000 per program PR[1]–PR[100] 
J P[1:Home] 100% FINE ;         ! Local taught position
L PR[1:Offset_Pos] 500mm/sec FINE ;  ! Global computed position
PR[1]=P[1] ;                    ! Copy P into PR

When to use which:

  • P[i] for fixed, taught points (home, pick, place)
  • PR[i] for positions calculated at runtime (offsets, patterns, sensor-based corrections)

Part 5: Program Logic

TP Program Structure

/PROG PICK_PLACE
/ATTR
OWNER    = ;
COMMENT  = "Simple Pick and Place";
/MN
   1:  ! Initialize ;
   2:  DO[1:Gripper]=OFF ;
   3:  J P[1:Home] 100% FINE ;
   4:  ! Pick sequence ;
   5:  L P[2:Pick_App] 500mm/sec FINE ;
   6:  L P[3:Pick] 100mm/sec FINE ;
   7:  DO[1:Gripper]=ON ;
   8:  WAIT  .50(sec) ;
   9:  L P[2:Pick_App] 500mm/sec FINE ;
  10:  ! Place sequence ;
  11:  L P[4:Place_App] 500mm/sec FINE ;
  12:  L P[5:Place] 100mm/sec FINE ;
  13:  DO[1:Gripper]=OFF ;
  14:  WAIT  .30(sec) ;
  15:  L P[4:Place_App] 500mm/sec FINE ;
  16:  J P[1:Home] 100% FINE ;
/END

Conditional Logic

IF/THEN/ELSE

IF DI[1]=ON, JMP LBL[10] ;
! DI[1] is OFF, do this:
DO[2]=ON ;
JMP LBL[20] ;
LBL[10] ;
! DI[1] is ON, do this:
DO[3]=ON ;
LBL[20] ;

SELECT (Case Statement)

SELECT R[1]=1, JMP LBL[1] ;
       =2, JMP LBL[2] ;
       =3, JMP LBL[3] ;
       ELSE, JMP LBL[99] ;

Pendant: [INST] button

Instruction Path
IF (register) 3 IF/SELECT → 1
IF (input) 3 IF/SELECT → 2
SELECT 3 IF/SELECT → 3
Label 5 JMP/LBL → 2
Jump 5 JMP/LBL → 1

Loops and Waiting

FOR Loop

FOR R[1]=1 TO 10 ;
  ! Repeat 10 times
  L P[1] 500mm/sec CNT100 ;
  L P[2] 500mm/sec CNT100 ;
ENDFOR ;

WAIT Instructions

WAIT  1.00(sec) ;           ! Wait 1 second
WAIT DI[1]=ON ;             ! Wait for input
WAIT DI[1]=ON TIMEOUT,LBL[99] ;

Labels and Jumps

LBL[1] ;
  ! Do something
  IF R[1]<10, JMP LBL[1] ;  ! Loop back

Pendant: [INST] button

Instruction Path
FOR page 3 → 1 FOR/ENDFOR
ENDFOR page 3 → 1 FOR/ENDFOR
WAIT (time) 4 WAIT
WAIT (condition) 4 WAIT
I/O (DO) 2 I/O
Registers 1 Registers

Loop Patterns: WHILE and DO-WHILE

FANUC TP has no native WHILE keyword — build it with LBL/IF/JMP:

WHILE pattern (check before body):

LBL[1] ;
  IF R[1]>=10, JMP LBL[2] ;  ! exit condition
  ! --- loop body ---
  L PR[1] 500mm/sec FINE ;
  R[1]=R[1]+1 ;
  JMP LBL[1] ;                ! loop back
LBL[2] ;

Runs zero or more times.

DO-WHILE pattern (check after body):

LBL[1] ;
  ! --- loop body ---
  WAIT DI[1]=ON ;
  CALL PROCESS_PART ;
  R[1]=R[1]+1 ;
  IF R[1]<10, JMP LBL[1] ;   ! loop back

Runs at least once.

Registers and Data

Registers (R[ ])

R[1]=0 ;              ! Set to zero
R[1]=R[1]+1 ;         ! Increment
IF R[1]>10, JMP LBL[5] ;

Position Registers (PR[ ])

PR[1]=P[1] ;          ! Copy position
PR[1,1]=100.0 ;       ! Set X component
L PR[1] 500mm/sec FINE ; ! Move to PR

Using Math

R[3]=R[1]+R[2] ;      ! Addition
R[4]=R[1]*2 ;         ! Multiplication
R[5]=SQRT[R[1]] ;     ! Square root

Pulse Output (single timed pulse, useful for signaling):

DO[2:Done]=PULSE,0.5sec ;

Frames: UTOOL and UFRAME

User Frame (UFRAME) — where is the work?

  • Defines the workpiece coordinate system
  • All taught positions are relative to it
  • Change UFRAME = all positions shift together
UFRAME_NUM=2 ;   ! Switch to frame 2

If your part moves to a new fixture, just re-teach the frame — not every point.

Tool Frame (UTOOL) — what’s on the wrist?

  • Defines the tool center point (TCP)
  • Calibrate once per tool/gripper
  • Affects all motion and position display
UTOOL_NUM=3 ;     ! Switch to tool 3

Wrong UTOOL = robot goes to wrong place. Always verify which tool is active before teaching.

Subroutines with CALL

Break programs into reusable parts — just like functions in Python:

/PROG MAIN
   1:  CALL PICK ;         ! Run the PICK subprogram
   2:  CALL PLACE ;        ! Run the PLACE subprogram
   3:  JMP LBL[1] ;        ! Loop
/END
/PROG PICK
   1:  L P[1:Approach] 500mm/sec FINE ;
   2:  L P[2:Grasp] 100mm/sec FINE ;
   3:  DO[1:Gripper]=ON ;
   4:  WAIT  .30(sec) ;
   5:  L P[1:Approach] 500mm/sec FINE ;
/END

Use CALL to keep programs short and reusable — just like functions in code.

Position Register Math (Offsets)

PR components: PR[n,1]=X, PR[n,2]=Y, PR[n,3]=Z

Offset a position by 50mm in X:

PR[10]=P[1:Base] ;        ! Copy base position
PR[10,1]=PR[10,1]+50.0 ;  ! Shift X by 50mm
L PR[10] 200mm/sec FINE ;  ! Move to offset position

3×3 grid palletizing pattern:

PR[10]=P[1:Corner] ;        ! Grid origin
FOR R[1]=0 TO 2 ;
  FOR R[2]=0 TO 2 ;
    PR[10,1]=P[1:Corner,1]+R[2]*50 ;  ! X offset
    PR[10,2]=P[1:Corner,2]+R[1]*50 ;  ! Y offset
    L PR[10] 300mm/sec FINE ;
    CALL PLACE ;
  ENDFOR ;
ENDFOR ;

Built-in Offset Instructions

Instead of manually computing PR math, FANUC provides dedicated offset instructions:

General Offset (relative to User Frame):

! Set offset condition
OFFSET CONDITION PR[10] ;
! Move with offset applied
L P[1] 500mm/sec FINE Offset ;

! Or apply directly:
L P[1] 500mm/sec FINE Offset,PR[10] ;

Shifts the target point by PR[10] values in the active User Frame directions.

Tool Offset (relative to Tool Frame):

! Set offset condition
TOOL_OFFSET CONDITION PR[20] ;
! Move with tool offset applied
L P[1] 500mm/sec FINE Tool_Offset ;

! Or apply directly:
L P[1] 500mm/sec FINE Tool_Offset,PR[20] ;

Shifts along the tool axes — useful for approach/retract along the tool Z.

Key difference: General Offset shifts in world/user frame directions. Tool Offset shifts in the tool’s own coordinate system (e.g., approach 50mm above a surface along the gripper axis regardless of orientation).

Part 6: Practical Applications

Pick and Place with Sensor Check

/PROG PICK_WITH_CHECK
   1:  J P[1:Home] 100% FINE ;
   2:  LBL[1] ;
   3:  ! Wait for part present
   4:  WAIT DI[1:Part_Sensor]=ON ;
   5:  ! Pick sequence
   6:  L P[2:Pick_App] 500mm/sec FINE ;
   7:  L P[3:Pick] 100mm/sec FINE ;
   8:  DO[1:Gripper]=ON ;
   9:  WAIT  .30(sec) ;
  10:  ! Verify grip
  11:  IF DI[2:Grip_Confirm]=OFF, JMP LBL[99] ;
  12:  L P[2:Pick_App] 500mm/sec FINE ;
  13:  ! Place sequence
  14:  L P[4:Place_App] 500mm/sec CNT50 ;
  15:  L P[5:Place] 100mm/sec FINE ;
  16:  DO[1:Gripper]=OFF ;
  17:  WAIT  .20(sec) ;
  18:  L P[4:Place_App] 500mm/sec FINE ;
  19:  JMP LBL[1] ;  ! Loop forever
  20:  LBL[99] ;
  21:  ! Error: grip failed
  22:  DO[3:Error_Light]=ON ;
  23:  PAUSE ;
/END

I/O Handshaking with External Device

The diagram shows the protocol. In TP code:

DO[1:Robot_Ready]=ON ;              ! 1. Signal "ready"
WAIT DI[1:Part_Ready]=ON ;          ! 2. Wait for conveyor
DO[1:Robot_Ready]=OFF ;             ! 3. Acknowledge
! ... pick operation ...
DO[2:Pick_Done]=PULSE,0.5sec ;      ! 4. Signal "done"

Debugging I/O & Common Mistakes

On the Teach Pendant:

  1. I/O Screen: MENU → I/O → Digital
    • View all DI/DO states
    • Force outputs ON/OFF (in manual mode)
  2. Status Screen: Shows active I/O

Common I/O Issues:

Symptom Likely Cause
Input always OFF Wiring, sensor fault, wrong type
Input always ON Stuck sensor, wrong NO/NC logic
Output no effect Load not connected, fuse blown
Intermittent Loose connection, noise

Common TP Programming Mistakes:

  • Forgetting WAIT after gripper ON/OFF — gripper hasn’t closed yet when robot moves
  • Using J motion near workpiece — unpredictable path may collide
  • Missing FINE at pick/place — robot blends past the target
  • Wrong sensor logic — NO sensor reads opposite of what you expect
  • No grip confirmation — robot moves with no part

Summary

Key Concepts:

  1. Digital I/O: The interface between robot and world
  2. Sensors: Inductive, photoelectric, mechanical - choose by application
  3. Safety: Layered protection, fail-safe design
  4. Program Logic: Motion commands, conditionals, loops

Exit Ticket

Scenario: You need to write a FANUC TP program that:

  • Waits for a part sensor (DI[1]) to turn ON
  • Moves to the pick position with Joint motion
  • Closes the gripper (DO[1]=ON) and waits 0.5 seconds
  • Moves to the place position with Linear motion
  • Opens the gripper (DO[1]=OFF)

Write the TP program (5-7 lines).

Exit Ticket: Solution

   1: WAIT DI[1:Part_Ready]=ON ;
   2: J P[1] 100% FINE ;
   3: DO[1:Gripper]=ON ;
   4: WAIT  .50(sec) ;
   5: L P[2] 200mm/sec FINE ;
   6: DO[1:Gripper]=OFF ;
   7: WAIT  .50(sec) ;

Key points:

  • WAIT for sensor before moving (don’t pick air!)
  • Joint (J) for fast travel to pick, Linear (L) for precise place
  • FINE termination at pick/place (must stop exactly)
  • WAIT after gripper commands (mechanical delay)
